general.temas: Air traffic disruptions and FAA infrastructure problems dominate four front pages. Also recurring are the large waves in California, the ban on new wealth taxes in that state, and conflicts at universities. The New York Post stands out in particular for its American football coverage.
general.motivo_crispacion: Tension stems from Iran’s attacks on Bahrain and suspicions of threats linked to Iran in Europe. In the United States, prominent issues include questions about the commerce secretary’s family interests, disagreement over a Florida law, and a legal dispute over a golf course in Washington. Aviation failures are generating concern and criticism, although much of the coverage is informational. Sports, environmental and everyday-life stories temper the overall mood.

The New York Times.resumen:
- Jensen Huang’s resignation from Nvidia and the reaction in Taiwan feature in two headlines.
- Several stories address air traffic disruptions, air traffic control infrastructure and aviation safety.
- The front page covers Iranian attacks on Bahrain, concern in Europe and questions about the case of an Israeli hostage.
- It examines chip rules championed by Lutnick and an upcoming meeting of tech executives in China.
- Democrats are beginning to look ahead to the 2028 presidential election.
The New York Times.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “secret,” “fall,” “spy games” and references to “fragile” technologies add drama, but there is no clear appeal to the people against the elites.
The New York Times.sesgo: The selection emphasizes technological and security vulnerabilities, potential conflicts of interest and criticism of aviation management. No clear ideological bias is apparent from the headlines provided.

The Washington Post.resumen:
- The nationwide air traffic disruption caused thousands of cancellations; authorities expect a return to normal by late Sunday.
- The installation of a router and work on wiring are cited as causes of the disruption, after years of warnings about risks associated with repairs.
- A case at Tulane focuses attention on possible gaps in university disciplinary systems when dealing with rape allegations.
- The FBI is investigating a bomb found at an Illinois ethanol plant, which prompted evacuations.
- Also prominent are a campaign on property rights, a conflict over a Florida law, and cultural, political and weather news.
The Washington Post.motivo_populismo: The tone is mostly informational, although expressions such as “rush” to resume flights and “battered beaches” add drama.
The Washington Post.sesgo: The front page gives particular weight to air traffic disruptions and possible institutional responsibility. It also pays attention to legal and social conflicts, without an unmistakable partisan orientation.

The Wall Street Journal.resumen:
- A judge has blocked, for now, the closure of a public golf course in Washington that the Trump administration wanted to transform.
- Christian schools and universities oppose a tax proposal on racial preferences.
- Air traffic disruptions will continue through the weekend despite the lifting of the nationwide flight suspension.
- The United States loses its measles-free status after a surge in cases; in New Orleans, more than 100 people are rescued from a river cruise ship struck by an oil tanker.
- Several stories address university conflicts and trends; in California, voters approve a ban on wealth taxes.
The Wall Street Journal.motivo_populismo: The tone is mostly informational, although expressions such as “historic surge” and “miracle on the Mississippi” add drama; there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
The Wall Street Journal.sesgo: The front page focuses on the United States and pays particular attention to education and institutional conflicts. The selection and wording show no clear partisan bias.

Los Angeles Times.resumen:
- The FAA breakdown causes cancellations and delays; its cause is being investigated ahead of the Thanksgiving travel surge.
- Heavy surf forces the closure of the Manhattan Beach pier; a train fatally strikes two people in Ventura County.
- Police are investigating gunfire that caused no injuries at an Ontario shopping center and a possible violent double death in San Dimas.
- Voters approve Proposition 42, which bans new taxes on personal property, with 96% of votes counted.
- Also prominent are sea turtle hatchlings in California, an ice cream theft, a documentary about Russell Brand and an FBI operation against a North Korean hacking group.
Los Angeles Times.motivo_populismo: Expressions such as “airport nightmares,” “historic meltdown” and “unprecedented chaos” rely on drama, although there is no apparent appeal to the people against the elites.
Los Angeles Times.sesgo: The selection prioritizes California news, incidents and transportation disruptions, with some dramatic headlines. No clear political orientation is apparent; the Russell Brand piece is explicitly presented as commentary.

New York Post.resumen:
- Previews, predictions and betting on NFL games predominate.
- Several stories analyze players and teams, including the Raiders, the 49ers and the Rams.
- The Big Ten standings highlight former JMU coaches.
- Italy fines Meta over access to Android users’ photo galleries; another headline addresses the repression of Christians in China.
- Lauren Miller recounts her experience during her mother’s battle with Alzheimer’s disease.
New York Post.motivo_populismo: A sporting and informational tone predominates, although expressions such as “sneaky access,” “unleashes a sweeping crackdown” and “heartbreaking” add drama and sensationalism.
New York Post.sesgo: The selection clearly favors American sports and predictions, with secondary attention to technology, religion and entertainment. No clear political orientation is apparent from these headlines.

opiniones.comunista:
I see the air traffic shutdown as more than a technical failure: it reveals aging public infrastructure on which millions of people depend and whose modernization cannot be pushed aside. The specific causes are still being investigated, but the political lesson is clear: we need sustained investment, sufficient staffing and public control, not the subordination of essential services to private profit.

I am also concerned that California has approved a ban on new wealth taxes after a campaign funded by billionaires. Respecting the vote does not prevent us from questioning the economic power that influences the debate and protects accumulated wealth.

As a communist, I believe working people should have real power over economic decisions. Collective ownership of strategic sectors and robust public services would allow resources to be directed toward common needs, rather than leaving their fate in the hands of big capital.
opiniones.anarquista:
The air traffic shutdown shows how fragile infrastructure on which millions depend can be. I do not believe the answer is to give more power to officials or companies: those who maintain and use these systems should be able to organize and oversee them directly, with transparency, technical coordination and sufficient resources. Safety requires shared knowledge, not blind obedience.

I also distrust chip rules drafted by a secretary whose former business ties intersect with their effects. There is no need to assume corruption has been proven to question a system that concentrates public decisions and private business in the same hands. And, although I respect the outcome of the California vote on wealth taxes, I do not confuse freedom with the power of the richest to organize other people’s lives. I prefer self-managed communities, mutual aid and freedom for all, not privileges for a few.
opiniones.liberal:
I see the collapse of air traffic control as a warning: a state that tries to do too much cannot afford to neglect its essential functions. If infrastructure is aging and warnings are mounting, it is not enough to ask travelers for patience. We must demand accountability, evaluate alternatives and make room for competition where it improves service without compromising safety.

I also welcome California’s ban on new taxes on personal wealth. Taxing assets, regardless of the income they generate, penalizes saving and investment. I prefer low taxes and limited government that leaves people free to decide what to do with what is theirs. That freedom, in turn, demands responsibility: from those who run companies as well as from officials who regulate sectors to which they have ties. A free market must not be confused with privileges granted by those in power.
opiniones.extrema_derecha:
The air traffic shutdown reveals an uncomfortable truth: a country that cannot keep its essential infrastructure running is neglecting its sovereignty. For years, warnings were issued about the risks associated with repairs; now thousands of travelers are paying the price. I demand accountability, investment in reliable systems and fewer bureaucratic excuses, whoever is in power.

I am also concerned that the chip rules could benefit former clients of the commerce secretary’s family business. Technology policy must protect national interests, not raise suspicions of favoritism. And ahead of the summit planned in China, the United States should negotiate from a position of strength, without sacrificing its security for the commercial opportunities of a few large companies.

I also welcome the beatification of the martyrs of Georgia: our religious traditions deserve respect and a visible place in public life.
opiniones.centro:
The air traffic chaos reminds me that competent government is not a luxury: it is a condition for the economy and everyday life to function. Modernizing air traffic control requires sustained investment, but also rigorous testing, transparency and independent oversight. It is not enough to buy new technology if we cannot integrate it without jeopardizing the service. Democrats and Republicans should agree on a gradual, verifiable plan.

I am also concerned that the commerce secretary is pushing rules that could affect clients of his former company. I do not assume any wrongdoing has been proven, but public trust requires clarifying potential conflicts of interest and removing the appropriate people from decision-making. Likewise, the resurgence of measles calls for an evidence-based public health response. A dynamic market needs institutions capable of protecting everyone.
